newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Record premiums seen in Kuwait term naphtha talks.
newsitem.headline: Record premiums seen in Kuwait term naphtha talks.

text.p: Kuwait Petroleum Corp's (KPC) term talks with its Asian buyers for more than two million tonnes of full range naphtha sales are generating record high premiums for supplies from March 1997 to February 1998, industry sources said on Thursday.
"It is in the teens," was all a KPC source was willing to divulge.
Traders said bids were at $12 to $14 per tonne over Mideast naptha free-on-board spot quotes, while KPC was asking for a premium of $15-$16.
The levels were much higher than Kuwait's price settled in its its last round of talks for supplies for August 1996-September 1997 at a $7.90 premium.
Levels were even higher than the last price settled by Bahrain in January at a $11 premium for light naphtha lifting June-December 1997.

Naptha term prices already were on the rise, with Asian buyers settling in October last year a higher premium for Saudi Aramco's A-180 lifting in the first half of this year of $6.50, up $2.50 to $3.10.
But the high price was not deterring any buyers from renewing contracts and some were even asking for an increase in volume, the sources said.
"In fact, some parties want to increase volumes because naphtha is so tight, especially for such full range naphtha," said a Japanese trader.
Traders expected supplies to tighten with the commissioning three new ethylene crackers in Singapore, Thailand and India this year.

"The three crackers will require over six million tonnes (per-year) of naphtha as feedstock," assessed a Japanese trader. "That is too big a quantity. End-users see the situation as tighter ... and they will have to pay."
"It (the $15 premium) is achievable if there's really a shortage and the market is tight," said one term buyer. "But the Japanese will find that a high price to pay."
The KPC source told Reuters the conclusion would only be known next week when term contracts are due to be finalised.
